content: Transmembrane protein 261 (TMEM261) is a protein encoded by the TMEM261 gene, which is located on chromosome 9 at position 9p24.1. This gene is also referred to as C9ORF123, DMAC1, Chromosome 9 Open Reading Frame 123, and Transmembrane Protein C9orf123. The TMEM261 gene spans 91,891 base pairs on the reverse strand of the chromosome. Its neighboring gene, PTPRD, is located at 9p23-p24.3, also on the reverse strand, and encodes protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type delta. TMEM261 contains two exons and one intron, and it has six primary transcript variants. The largest mRNA transcript variant is 742 base pairs long, encoding a protein of 129 amino acids with a molecular weight of 13,500 Daltons. The smallest coding transcript variant is 381 base pairs long, encoding a protein of 69 amino acids with a molecular weight of 6,100 Daltons. The TMEM261 protein itself is composed of 112 amino acids and has a molecular weight of approximately 11.8 kDa. Its predicted isoelectric point is 10.2, and its post-translational modification value is 9.9. Structurally, TMEM261 contains a domain of unknown function (DUF4536), which is predicted to be a helical membrane-spanning domain approximately 45 amino acids in length (spanning residues Cys47 to Ser92). Additionally, two other transmembrane helical domains are predicted, one spanning 18 amino acids (Val52 to Ala69) and the other spanning 23 amino acids (Pro81 to Ala102). A low-complexity region is also present, spanning 25 amino acids (Thr14 to Ala39). The tertiary structure of TMEM261 has not yet been determined, but its secondary structure is primarily composed of coiled-coil regions, with beta strands and alpha helices located within the transmembrane regions and the domain of unknown function. The N-terminal region of TMEM261 is disordered and contains the low-complexity region, which is not highly conserved among orthologues. TMEM261 undergoes several post-translational modifications. Most variants of the protein contain an N-myristoylation domain. Specifically, the N-terminal glycine residue (Gly2) undergoes myristoylation, and threonine at position 31 (Thr31) is phosphorylated. TMEM261 interacts with several other proteins. Protein-protein interactions include those with NAAA, APP, and ARHGEF38. RNA-protein interactions involve QTRT1 and HNRNPD, while DNA-protein interactions include ZC4H2 and ZNF454. Additionally, transcription factor binding sites have been predicted for TMEM261, including one binding site for MEF2C, a monocyte-specific enhancer involved in muscle cell regulation, particularly in the cardiovascular system, and two binding sites for GATA1, a transcription factor involved in erythroblast development. TMEM261 is ubiquitously expressed in humans and is detected in nearly all tissue types. It exhibits tissue-enriched gene expression compared to housekeeping genes, with the highest expression levels observed in the heart (94% relative expression, particularly in heart fibroblast cells), thymus (90% relative expression), and thyroid (93% relative expression, particularly in thyroid glandular cells). In cancer cells, TMEM261 expression is intermediate to high in breast, colorectal, ovarian, skin, urothelial, and head and neck cancers. The precise function of TMEM261 remains unknown. However, gene amplification and rearrangements involving its locus have been associated with various cancers, including colorectal cancer, breast cancer, and lymphomas. From an evolutionary perspective, TMEM261 orthologues and homologues are limited to vertebrates. The oldest known homologue dates back to cartilaginous fishes, which diverged from humans approximately 462.5 million years ago. The primary structure of TMEM261 shows higher conservation in mammals, but the domain of unknown function (DUF4536) and the C-terminal region are highly conserved across all orthologues, including distant homologues. TMEM261 has no known paralogues.
